questions.q: What does the line `Integer orderCount = 10;` do, per this lesson?
options: It only prints the number 10 to the debug log
It declares a variable named orderCount, states it will hold an Integer, and assigns it an initial value of 10, all in one statement
It creates ten separate variables
It permanently fixes the value 10 so it can never change later
questions.explain: The lesson describes this single line as doing three things at once: declaring the variable, stating its type, and giving it an initial value -- and notes the value can still be changed later with a plain assignment.

questions.q: How does this lesson define Apex as 'strongly and statically typed'?
options: Every variable's type is declared up front and fixed for its lifetime (static), and the compiler only allows operations valid for that type (strong)
Variable types can change freely at any point while the program runs
Apex has no concept of data types at all
Strongly typed means variables must be written in all capital letters
questions.explain: Static typing means a variable's declared type is fixed; strong typing means the compiler enforces that only valid operations for that type are allowed -- together this catches a category of mistakes at compile time rather than at runtime.

questions.q: Per this lesson, how are String literals written in Apex?
options: In double quotes, exactly like 'Jordan Lee' written as "Jordan Lee"
In single quotes, like 'Jordan Lee', not double quotes
Without any quotation marks at all
In square brackets
questions.explain: The lesson specifically flags that Apex String values are written in single quotes, not double quotes, as a common trip-up for developers coming from languages that use double quotes for strings.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say Decimal is typically preferred over Double for representing money in Apex?
options: Decimal and Double are exactly identical in every respect with no difference at all
Double cannot hold a number with a decimal point
Decimal is the type Apex code typically reaches for when precision matters, since currency math that silently loses a fraction of a cent is a real problem
Decimal is the only type that can be declared with the `var` keyword
questions.explain: The lesson notes both Double and Decimal hold numbers with decimal points, but Decimal is favored for money specifically because precision matters for currency calculations.

questions.q: What value does a declared-but-unassigned Apex variable (like `Id accountId;`) hold by default?
options: Zero
An empty string
False
Null -- meaning no value at all, which is a common source of runtime errors if treated as if it held a real value
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that an unassigned Apex variable defaults to null, not to a type-specific 'empty' value like zero or false, and that treating null as a real value is a frequent source of runtime errors.
